discussions.name: NWS Seattle
synopsis: A strong frontal system will impact Western Washington this evening into Thursday, bringing widespread rain, gusty winds, and increased threat for coastal flooding. Precipitation chances will linger into Friday with a weaker system. A brief break in precipitation this weekend as a weak ridge builds over the Pacific Northwest. An active weather pattern resumes next week.
hydrology: A frontal system will bring an additional 2 to 4 inches of rainfall to the region through Thursday, with snow levels rising as high as 6000-7500 feet. The bulk of the moisture is expected over the Olympic Peninsula and along the coast. While area rivers will likely experience rises, no widespread river flooding is expected.

The exception is the Skokomish River, where a River Flood Warning remains in effect through Friday. The Skokomish will rise above flood stage later today and is expected to peak in moderate flood stage late tonight into early Thursday morning. The Skokomish is expected to fall below flood stage on Friday, with additional rises possible into next week.

The incoming heavy rainfall through Thursday may also pose a hazard to the Bear Gulch burn scar, which has been sensitive to precipitation so far this winter season. A handful of small landslides have already occurred on the burn scar, and additional landslides in this area cannot be ruled out this week as heavy rain continues over the Olympic Peninsula.

sections.title: Short term (tonight through Friday night)
paragraphs: Current radar showing widespread rain over W WA this evening. Highest reflectivities and therefore heaviest precip remains mainly over the western half of the CWA...from the coast to the west side of the Sound. 5 PM PST climate report showing that Hoquiam and Quillayute have already exceeded 1 inch of rainfall and likely to see that much more by midnight. As the first batch of higher reflectivity rainfall is reaching the Sound now, will be curious to see if that intensity remains in place for the eastern portion of the area. Latest QPF definitely shows an increase in rainfall for this eastern half but still a significant drop-off from what has been and will be seen on the west side...which is typical.
All in all, inherited headlines and forecast remain on track, thus no need for any evening updates. For additional forecast details, please refer to the Previous Discussion section below.  18

From Previous Discussion...Latest radar imagery shows rain continuing to move across portions of Western Washington this afternoon as a strong frontal system quickly prepares to push onshore starting this evening. Rain will start filling in along the coast this afternoon and spread into the interior later this evening. Breezy conditions are already present across the region, with latest obs showing gusts 20-30 mph. Winds will only continue to increase this evening and late tonight. The strongest winds will be concentrated along the immediate coastline, with gusts up to 60 mph. As a result, the Wind Advisory for the coastal communities for Grays Harbor, Jefferson, and Clallam Counties has been upgraded to a High Wind Warning. Winds Advisories remain in effect elsewhere. Across the Northern Interior and San Juan Islands gusts to 50 mph are expected. Along Puget Sound gusts to 45 mph are expected. Winds will gradually subside Thursday evening.

Snow levels in the Cascades will range between 5000-6000 feet with lower snow levels in the Northern Cascades Thursday morning. The majority of the snow is expected to fall overnight into Thursday, with 8-16 inches possible in the Northern Cascades. Moreover, the atmosphere will become destabilized Thursday morning for the chances of scattered thunderstorms. Latest guidance suggests the highest chances (20-25%) are along the coast and the Olympic Peninsula. Elsewhere, chances for thunderstorms are slightly lower at 15% or less. Rain chances continue on Friday as a shortwave trough moves across Western Washington.

As has been the case in recent days, coastal flooding will continue to be the headline-making hazard as some of the years highest astronomical tides combine with storm surge and high surf to produce some significant tidal anomalies and impacts to coastal communities. Coastal flooding impacts are expected to peak along the coast today, with the greatest impacts for the inner waters expected early Thursday before astronomical tides gradually weaken.

sections.title: Long term (Saturday through Wednesday)
paragraphs: There is good agreement between ensemble guidance that a weak upper level ridge will develop offshore late Friday and build over the Pacific Northwest this weekend for a break in from precipitation. The pattern becomes active once again heading into next week.

sections.title: Aviation
paragraphs: VFR conditions continue to prevail across most of western Washington, with the exception of the coast with continuing MVFR conditions this evening. Widespread rain will continue across the area overnight as a frontal system will traverse across the area early Thursday morning. Ceilings will likely mostly remain VFR, except around the time of frontal passage for a brief period of MVFR cigs. Rain will at time bring reductions in visibility to 3-5 SM in heavier rain. Cigs will then become broken low-end VFR or high end of MVFR through much of the day Thursday as precipitation becomes more showery. Lower ceilings will likely be associated with showers passing over the terminals. There is a low (15-25%) chance of thunderstorms across the area during the day Thursday, however confidence in timing/occurrence is too low to put into the TAFs at this time.

Breezy winds S/SE will continue to increase this evening, peaking overnight into early Thursday morning. The strongest winds will be along the coast with gusts up to 50 kt possible. Terminals north of PAE will also see gusty winds with gusts to 40 kt. As for Puget Sound terminals, gusts to 35 kt are expected. Gusty winds will continue through much of the day on Thursday was winds turn more SW, but will begin to decrease Thursday evening.

KSEA...VFR conditions continue this evening with rain. Limitations in visibility at times possible overnight in the heaviest rain. The most likely period of MVFR cigs is around 10-15Z overnight as the front passes through. Ceilings will become more broken and low-end VFR as precipitation becomes showery, with lower ceilings associated with passing showers over the terminal. There is a low (around 15%) chance of thunderstorms through Thursday afternoon. Winds will continue to increase into the overnight hours, with the strongest winds expected between 10Z-15Z with sustained winds of 15-20 kt and gusts to 35 kt. Winds will remain breezy Thursday afternoon out of the S/SW with gusts to 25 kt. Winds will slowly ease Thursday evening.

sections.title: Marine
paragraphs: A strong frontal system will cross area waters this afternoon into Thursday morning, bringing another round of strong winds and elevated seas to area waters. A Storm Warning remains in effect over the coastal waters, with Gale Warnings covering nearly all inner water zones to cover gusty winds with the front as it pushes inland. Thunderstorms are also favored to develop over the coastal waters early Thursday and move inland towards the inner waters throughout the day, producing localized lightning, gusty winds, and small hail.

Winds will die down across the waters by Thursday evening, with a Small Craft Advisory covering the coastal waters for both winds and elevated seas. A weak weather system is now favored to move into the region on Friday, but impacts should be minimal. High pressure will likely build over the waters over the weekend, allowing winds and seas to ease outside of a weak westerly push through the Strait of Juan de Fuca late Saturday into Sunday. The next system moving into the region on Monday is expected to bring another round of breezy winds, mainly for the coastal waters and into the Strait of Juan de Fuca. Additional headlines are likely, with active weather continuing into next week.

Seas generally around 15 to 21 feet today will continue to stay within that range into Thursday, and will start subsiding late Thursday into Friday to around 10 to 15 feet. Seas will lower even further by late Friday into Saturday, where we could see seas get below 10 feet through the weekend. Seas are favored to rise above 10 feet into next week.

discussions.name: NWS Portland
synopsis: An atmospheric river will bring heavy rain and increasing winds to the area tonight into Thanksgiving, with the strongest winds expected at the coast early Thanksgiving morning. Coastal and marine weather hazards remain the primary concern as high winds and rough seas coincide with King Tides, raising the chances for coastal flooding and dangerous sneaker waves. After a brief break from rain Thursday evening, another round of steady rain is expected Friday morning and afternoon with an incoming low pressure system. Mainly dry weather is expected this weekend with breezy easterly winds in the western Columbia River Gorge and eastern Portland metro. Trending wet again late Sunday into Monday with rain and breezy winds.

sections.title: Discussion
paragraphs: Now through Tuesday night...Satellite imagery from early Wednesday afternoon revealed an area of strong low pressure centered around 500 miles offshore from Vancouver Island, with an elongated axis of abundant moisture along the south side of the low associated with an atmospheric river. This atmospheric river will take aim at southwest WA and northwest OR tonight into Thanksgiving morning, bringing widespread heavy rain and gusty winds to the area. GEFS and EPS ensemble IVT forecasts remain in good agreement for a strong atmospheric river, however the total duration is limited as the axis of heaviest rain will be progressively moving from north to south rather than stalling out over the area. As such, chances for river flooding are very low (<10% per HEFS guidance), especially given the fact that river levels leading into the event are relatively low. Total rain amounts with this system between tonight and late Thursday evening are forecast to reach 0.75-1.0 inches for most locations in the Willamette Valley and Portland/Vancouver metro, with 1-2.5 inches favored for the coast, coastal mountains, Cascades/foothills, and lower Columbia/Cowlitz Valley. Although these rain amounts are not enough to produce river flooding, hourly rain amounts upwards of 0.25 in/hr are possible Thursday morning (5-15% chance at any given lowland location between 1-8 AM PST Thursday, except 50-80% at the coast, per REFS guidance). Simulated reflectivity guidance from the RRFS hints at the potential development of a narrow cold frontal rain band as a cold front moves inland with the atmospheric river during that time, which would be the culprit for rain rates of this magnitude. While these rain rates are not overly concerning given the short ~1 hour duration they would most likely last at any given location, this is still high enough to result in minor urban flooding in low-lying areas with poor drainage and clogged storm drains. The most likely time period for the period of heaviest rain in the Portland metro is between 4-8 AM PST Thursday. Rain becomes gradually lighter thereafter, before persistent stratiform rain eases to light scattered showers in the wake of the cold frontal passage. Note snow levels with this system will be well above the Cascade passes, so those planning on traveling over the passes should expect rain rather than snow.

The cold frontal passage will also be accompanied by gusty southerly winds, especially at the coast and for higher elevations in the coastal mountains. Conditions will be windy at the coast between 10 PM PST Wednesday and 7 AM PST Thursday, which is when a High Wind Warning is in effect for beaches and headlands. The period of strongest winds are expected to occur between 3-7 AM PST Thursday when gusts up to 60 mph are expected on beaches and headlands. Although it will be also be windy for inland coastal communities, maximum gusts will be relatively weaker compared to beaches and headlands with gusts up to 50-55 mph. Higher elevations in the Coast Range can expect gusts up to approximately 50 mph. Those living in coastal communities should secure loose outdoor objects and be prepared for potential power outages. Beachgoers should exercise extreme caution as tidal overflow flooding, dangerous sneaker waves, and high winds will all be hazards. Coastal hazards are discussed below in the beach hazards section.

After a brief break from rain Thursday evening, another round of steady rain is expected Friday morning and afternoon with an incoming low pressure system. Model ensemble guidance varies in regards to the exact strength and track of this low, however guidance is at least in good agreement the central pressure with this low will be above 1000 mb with a track somewhere over northwest Oregon. With a baroclinic zone on the north side of the low within an area of cyclonic vorticity advection, favorable forcing for ascent will be in place. Given an increase in moisture as well, decent rain amounts of 0.8-2.0 inches are forecast with this system Thursday night through Friday night, with the highest amounts in the Cascades. While flooding is not expected with this system, Friday will be a wet day. A small subset of ensemble guidance produces a low that is just deep enough to result in a localized area of high winds on the south side of the low. The central Oregon coast has the highest chance of high winds with this system, however even there this outcome is unlikely (10-20% chance for max wind gusts over 55 mph south of Pacific City per NBM guidance). Chances for wind gusts over 55 mph in the Willamette Valley and Portland metro range between 1-5%. If this low probability scenario were to occur, winds would be blowing from south to north and downed trees and power outages would be a concern.

Mainly dry weather is expected this weekend with breezy easterly winds in the western Columbia River Gorge and eastern Portland metro as high pressure returns to the area. Abnormally strong easterly winds are not expected, as the surface pressure gradient between Troutdale and the Dalles is forecast to hover between -3 and -6 mb most of the time according to the EURO ensemble. Conditions trend wet again late Sunday into Monday with a 90% chance of rain and breezy offshore winds. Chances for rain decrease to 25-50% on Tuesday. Snow levels look to remain above pass level through Tuesday night, with no clear signal for accumulating snow on highway 26, Santiam Pass, or Willamette Pass. -23

sections.title: Aviation
paragraphs: Through 00z Friday...VFR conditions persist across the region this afternoon as a frontal system begins to approach the coastline. As this feature moves onshore and increasing showers turn to steady rain this evening and overnight, CIGs/VIS likely degrade to low end VFR to MVFR with a 40-60% chance for MVFR conditions at the coast 08-18z - 20-40% chance inland during the same time period. Steadier rain likely breaks to post-frontal showers NW to SE as the morning progresses with most sites reverting to showers 15-19z.

Southerly winds are already beginning to increase across the Willamette Valley, likely rising to around 10 kt with gusts peaking 20-27 kt peaking overnight. Expect more southeast winds in the Portland metro, strongest near the western entrance of the Columbia River Gorge, before shifting southerly as the front passes overnight. Along the coast, gusts peak as 30-40 kt this evening and overnight before decreasing Thursday morning.

In addition to the surface winds, increasing winds at 2 kft above the surface leads to periods of low-level wind shear at most terminals as well, highest as the frontal boundary passes overhead. Coastal terminals will see this peak speed-shear with 60-70 kt winds at 2 kft overnight, while Portland-area terminals see more directional shear given southeast winds at the surface and 30-50 kt winds at 2 kft, peaking 10-15z before the front passes and the wind shear threat subsides. Confidence is high in no further LLWS threat Thursday afternoon.

KPDX AND APPROACHES...VFR conditions are expected through most of the overnight period. Light rain showers increase this evening becoming steadier rain overnight into Thursday morning before turning to showers again. Southeast winds continue ahead of an approaching frontal boundary, shifting more out of the south nearing sunrise. Low-level wind shear persists through much of the night as winds at 2 kft increase out of the south-southwest to 30-40 kt after 03z, peaking around 50 kt in the 10-16z period Thursday. This concern quickly ends 16-18z. -99

sections.title: Marine
paragraphs: Conditions across the coastal waters remain extremely active into Thursday morning as another strong frontal system takes aim at the region this evening into the morning of Thanksgiving Day. Headed into the sunrise hours late this afternoon, expect winds to begin increasing, likely peaking between 10pm Wed and 4am Thursday. Widespread gale-force gusts are expected across the waters, with Gale Warnings in effect for most of the coastal waters including the Columbia River Bar through Thursday morning. The south-southwest wind direction will also support the development of a coastal jet along the north Oregon and south Washington coasts, resulting in locally higher winds within 10 NM of the coast from Cape Foulweather north to Cape Shoalwater, where a Storm Warning remains in effect. That said, isolated gusts of 50 kt will still be possible across the outer waters as the front arrives overnight, but these gusts did not appear frequent enough to expand the Storm Warning. Both wind- driven seas and the southwest swell will begin to ease by Thursday afternoon, although a period of Hazardous Seas persists through Thursday evening. While conditions appear calmer overall on Friday while seas continue to decrease, we're still monitoring a 10-20% chance that a rapidly developing surface low pressure will traverse the waters. Should this low probability but high impact scenario play out, yet another round of gusty south winds would be possible - uncertainty in this potential feature remains very high.

Improving marine conditions are then expected by Saturday during a break in the active weather. The progressive pattern is likely to bring further weather systems into the region from late Sunday into early next week. -99/36

sections.title: Beach hazards
paragraphs: A Coastal Flood Advisory remains in effect through Thursday, extending into Friday for the south Washington Coast thanks to the combination of King Tides and elevated seas leading to tidal overflow. Impacts during this period are most likely at high tide. Coastal residents in the warned area should be alert for rising water, and take appropriate action to protect life and property. There is also a continued moderate to high sneaker wave threat through Thursday into Friday. Beachgoers should exercise caution, stay far back from incoming waves, and remain observant of the ocean. Avoid logs, large rocks, and jetties.
